newsitem.title: UK: Blair says British Conservatives incompetent.
newsitem.headline: Blair says British Conservatives incompetent.

text.p: Opposition Labour leader Tony Blair, campaigning for Britain's May 1 general election, accused the ruling Conservatives on Monday of economic incompetence and said only his party could deliver the stability that would let the nation prosper.

Blair, whose party is enjoying a huge lead in opinion polls, rejected Conservative claims to credit for a currently booming economy. He reminded voters that, in 18 years of unbroken Conservative rule, Britain had been through two of the deepest recessions since World War Two.
In a speech to business people in London, he stressed his party's new-found faith in market forces and its rejection of such socialist concepts as nationalisation and high taxes.
Blair's speech came on the heels of Conservative charges that Labour had switched policy on two key economic issues.

Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, had on Sunday struck a more sceptical note on the European Union's planned single currency, saying that if Britain did not enter when it was set up in 1999 it would be unlikely to join a year or two later.

And on Monday, the party's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, refused to rule out proceeding with Conservative plans to privatise Britain's air traffic control industry. Labour had previously opposed the sell-off on safety grounds.
Blair said Britain had been on an economic rollercoaster since the Conservatives took power in 1979, with each boom being followed by bust.

"This instability is not a natural phenomenon visited upon us by the Almighty. It has been caused, to be frank, by the least competent management of any western economy in the past two decades," he said.
"There are underlying weaknesses in the economy that need to be addressed now if we are to avoid another bust and build prosperity that lasts," he added.
Blair said Labour had recognised that Britain's problems could not be solved simply by increasing the share of the economic cake spent by the government.
"The era of tax and spend is dead and buried. I accept the need for economic discipline and embrace the role of free enterprise in the economy. There will be no retreat from any of that," he said.

Brown's announcement on privatisation of the air traffic control system, and press suggestions it would sell off other government assets if it took power were immediately attacked by Kenneth Clarke, the chancellor of the exchequer (fiance minister).

"The opposition party changes its policy from day to day. What it shows is a party that has no set policies, that has no convictions, that has no principles and they are now making it up day by day as they go along," Clarke told reporters during a visit to Basildon, a key southeastern England constituency.
But the Conservatives, lagging Labour by more than 20 percentage points, according to the latest polls, found the election focus embarrassingly back on the issue of sleaze on Monday.

Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats said their candidates in the constituency of Neil Hamilton, a former trade minister accused of taking cash to ask parliamentary questions, had both agreed to step down in favour of an independent anti-sleaze candidate, BBC war reporter Martin Bell.
